title.en: The Ladder of the God: Ascending to Heaven by the Bull's Sinews
title.zh: 神之天梯：以天牛之筋登天

region.en: Sakkarah, Egypt (Pyramid Texts of Unas, Teta, Pepi I-II)
region.zh: 埃及薩卡拉（烏納斯、泰塔、佩皮金字塔文）

texts.period: Pyramid Texts, 5th-6th Dynasties, c. 2350-2175 BCE (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I, 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, the Ladder of the god (Pepi II 975 ff., Unas 579, Pepi I 192 ff.)

summary.en: The machinery of ascension: the ladder's wooden sides are shaped by the adze of the god Sashsa, its rungs made of the strong sinews of Kasut, the Bull of the Sky, fastened with knotted thongs from the hide of the god Utes, son of Hesat; Horus and Set, or Horus and Ra, set it up from earth to heaven, and as the dead god climbs, Isis is in front of him, Nephthys behind, Ap-uat opens the way, Shu bears him up, and Nut gives him her hands.
summary.zh: 登天之機器：天梯木欄由神沙沙之錛削成，橫檔乃天牛卡蘇特之強筋，以神烏特斯（赫薩特之子）之皮所結皮索縛定；荷魯斯與塞特（或荷魯斯與拉）置梯於天地之間；亡神攀之時，伊西斯在前，奈芙蒂斯在後，阿普-烏阿特開路，舒承之，努特伸手相迎。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal funerary texts via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions. OCR text cleaned of obvious scanning breaks.

passages.text: From the text of Pepi II (1. 975 ff.) we learn the tradition that the wooden sides of the ladder were shaped by an adze wielded by the god Sashsa, that the rungs were made of the strong sinews of Kasut, the Bull of the Sky, and that they were fastened in their places on the sides of the ladder with knotted thongs made from the hide of the god Utes, the son of Hesat. This divine ladder was set up from earth to heaven by Horus and Ra according to one legend, and according to another by Horus and Set.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III.

passages.text: The text of Unas says: 'Ra setteth up the ladder before Osiris, Horus setteth up the ladder before his father Osiris in his going to his spirit. One of them [standeth] on this side, and one of them on that side. Unas is between them.' In the text of Pepi I we find: 'Homage to thee, Ladder of the god! Homage to thee, Ladder of Set! Stand up, Ladder of the god, stand up, Ladder of Set, stand up, Ladder of Horus, whereby Osiris made his way into heaven.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III, quoting the Pyramid Texts of Unas and Pepi I.

passages.text: Lo, Khensu, lo, Aahes, Chief of the South-Land, lo, Tetun the Great, Chief of Ta-sti (Nubia), lo, Sept under his trees. They carry the ladder for this Pepi, they set up the ladder for this Pepi, they make firm the ladder for this Pepi. With the assistance of Horus and Set, Osiris stood on the ladder, and with their help he ascended and entered heaven. 'Every spirit and every god opened his hand to Pepi when he was on the ladder.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.

passages.text: When Osiris ascended the ladder, he 'was covered with the covering of Horus, he wore the apparel of Thoth, Isis was in front of him, Nephthys was behind him, Ap-uat opened the way for him, Shu bore him up, the Souls of An drew him up the steps of the ladder, and Nut gave him her hands.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III, quoting Pepi I l. 308.

title.en: Osiris the Word: 'The God Cometh, the God Cometh'
title.zh: 話語之奧西里斯：『神來了，神來了』

region.en: Heaven of the Egyptian Other World (symbolic pin, Abydos region)
region.zh: 埃及冥界天堂（象徵定位，阿拜多斯一帶）

texts.period: Pyramid Texts, 5th-6th Dynasties (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I, 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, Osiris in heaven

summary.en: The risen Osiris as creator-king in heaven: 'Osiris was the great word, and he gave orders to the Spirits, and he was the word of what cometh into being and what is not' — the Word through which all things in heaven came into being from non-existence; he transmits his odour to those he loves, his chosen sit on his shoulder, and at the proper moment his bodyguard cries out, 'The god Cometh, the god cometh, the god Cometh.'
summary.zh: 復起之奧西里斯為天上創制之王：『奧西里斯乃偉大之言語，彼向諸靈下令，彼乃『將有之物與未有之物』之言』——天堂萬有皆由此語自無而有；彼以己馨香授其所愛，所選者坐於其肩；其護衛依時齊呼：『神來了，神來了，神來了。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal funerary texts via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: He was 'Chief of the Powers,' he was 'master of heaven,' and he had the power to bestow 'life and well-being' upon those in heaven who went to him. He transmitted his own odour to those whom he loved, and his chosen ones sat on his shoulder. He sat upon a throne, holding sceptres emblematic of his various powers in his hands, and he was surrounded by his bodyguard, and nobles, and trusted servants, after the manner of an African king; at the proper moment these cried out, 'the god Cometh, the god cometh, the god cometh.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III.

passages.text: 'Heaven speaketh, and the earth trembleth, the Earth-god Keb quaketh, and the two regions of the god utter a noise,' and as a result the food whereon the gods and the blessed live is created. Osiris was the 'great word,' and he gave orders to the Spirits, and he was the 'word of what cometh into being and what is not.' In other words, Osiris the Word spake the words through which all things in heaven came into being from non-existence.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.

title.en: Osiris-Nepra, the Grain-god: To Plough Corn and Reap Barley
title.zh: 穀神奧西里斯-奈普拉：犁麥刈大麥

region.en: The Fields of Reeds (Sekhet-Aaru), Egyptian Other World

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, the Domains of Osiris

summary.en: Osiris in the Pyramid Texts is already the Grain-god: the deceased commands the Domains of Horus, of Set, and of Osiris — the Fields of Reeds — where Osiris makes the king 'to plough corn and to reap barley'; the blessed drinks the emissions of Osiris and eats what comes forth from him, living on the moisture and meal that are the body of the Grain-god.
summary.zh: 《金字塔文》中奧西里斯已是穀神：亡者向荷魯斯之領、塞特之領、奧西里斯之領下令——即蘆葦之田——彼使王『犁麥刈大麥』；蒙福者飲奧西里斯之分泌、食其所出，以穀神之濕與粉為食。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal funerary texts via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In the text of Unas the deceased is said to give the word of command to the Domains of Horus, the Domains of Set, and the Domains of Osiris, and from another passage the Domains of Osiris appear to have been also called 'Sekhet-Aaru,' i.e., 'The Fields of Reeds.' Among these 'fields of reeds' there must have been many fair fields wherein grain of various kinds was grown, for in the text of Pepi II, 1. 1316, it is said that Osiris makes Pepi 'to plough corn and to reap barley.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III.

passages.text: From this passage we are probably right in assuming that Osiris was, even at this early period, identified with the Grain-god Nepra. This view is, moreover, supported by the statement that the deceased drinks the emissions of Osiris and eats what comes forth from him, i.e., he lived on the moisture and meal which formed the Grain-god.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.

title.en: The Eye of Horus: Snatched from Set and Given to His Father
title.zh: 荷魯斯之眼：奪自塞特而獻於父

region.en: Egypt, the contest between Horus and Set (symbolic pin, Edfu-Abydos corridor)
region.zh: 埃及荷魯斯與塞特爭戰之地（象徵定位，埃德富-阿拜多斯走廊）

texts.period: Pyramid Texts (Pepi I 107 ff., Teta 70 ff.), 6th Dynasty (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I, 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, the Eye of Horus passages in full

summary.en: The theology of the eye in full: Set carried away the Eye of Horus, and while it was in his hands Horus was a dead god; Horus wrests it back, Thoth drives back the followers of Set, Keb sets his sandal on the head of the enemy, and the Eye is given to Osiris — 'thou obtainest a soul through it, thou gainest the mastery through it at the head of the Spirits' — 'Thou hast eaten the eye, thy body is fortified through it, thou livest thereby.'
summary.zh: 眼之神學全篇：塞特奪荷魯斯之眼，眼在其手則荷魯斯如死神；荷魯斯奪回，托特逐塞特之黨，蓋布以履踏敵首——眼乃獻於奧西里斯：『爾因之得魂，因之居諸靈之首而得權柄』——『爾食其眼，賴之身強，賴之得生。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal funerary texts via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Reference has been made above to the religious tradition in Egypt which asserted that the Eye of Horus had been carried away from him by Set, and that Horus only succeeded in wresting it from him after a fierce fight in which Set suffered serious injury. Now the Eye of Horus contained his soul, that is to say, his life, and during the period when his Eye was in the hands of Set he was a dead god.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III.

passages.text: 'Hail, thou Osiris Teta, Horus cometh, he embraceth thee. He causeth Thoth to drive back for thee the followers of Set, he bringeth them unto thee [as] prisoners. He hath turned backwards the heart of Set, [for] behold, he is stronger than he. — Keb looketh upon thy form, he setteth thee on thy throne. Keb bringeth thy two sisters to thy side, that is, Isis and Nephthys.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III, quoting the Pyramid Text of Teta (ll. 70 ff.).

passages.text: 'Keb hath set his sandal on the head of thine enemy [saying], Get thee back. Thy son Horus hath smitten him. He hath delivered (or, snatched away) his eye from him, he hath given it to thee, thou obtainest a soul through it, thou gainest the mastery through it at the head of the Spirits... Thy mother Nut hath stretched herself over thee in her name of Shet-pet. Horus hath seized Set, he hath set him under thee, he lifteth thee up, he is helpless under thee as Nurta. Thou art more majestic than he in thy name of Ta-tchesert.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.

passages.text: 'Thou hast eaten the eye, thy body is fortified through it, thy son Horus seized it for thee, thou livest thereby.' — Thus in the above extracts we have a definite statement about the means employed by Horus to bring his father Osiris to life.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.

title.en: Set the Brother Who Gives Life: The Conditional Spell
title.zh: 賜生之弟塞特：條件式咒文

region.en: Sakkarah, Egypt (Pyramid Texts of Unas and Pepi II)
region.zh: 埃及薩卡拉（烏納斯與佩皮二世金字塔文）

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, Set as the friend and foe of Osiris

summary.en: The strangest theological knot in the Pyramid Texts: in one place Set and Thoth are called the two brothers of the dead man, with Isis and Nephthys weeping for him; in another Set is called upon to give life to Osiris — 'if he liveth, this Unas liveth; if he dieth not, this Unas dieth not; if he begetteth, this Unas begetteth' — before other texts make him the arch-enemy whose defeat by Horus is described with satisfaction.
summary.zh: 《金字塔文》中最奇的神學紐結：一處稱塞特與托特為亡者之二兄，與伊西斯、奈芙蒂斯同哭；一處則呼塞特賜奧西里斯以生——『彼活則烏納斯活；彼不死則烏納斯不死；彼生則烏納斯生』——而其他文本復以其為死敵，樂述荷魯斯之勝。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal funerary texts via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions. The ambivalence of Set is a famous crux of Egyptian theology.

passages.text: The dismemberment of the body was the work of a god called Set, who, curiously enough, appears at one time to be a friend of the dead man, and at another to be his bitter foe. Thus, in one place, Set and Thoth are called his two brothers, and they are mentioned in connection with Isis and Nephthys who weep for him.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III.

passages.text: In another, Set is called upon to give life to Osiris and to make him live, for, continues the text, 'if he liveth, this Unas liveth; if he dieth not, this Unas dieth not; if he is not destroyed, this Unas is not destroyed; if he begetteth not, this Unas begetteth not; if he begetteth, this Unas begetteth.' On the other hand, we have in the text of Teta (1. 170 ff.) definite statements that Set is the arch-enemy of Osiris, as he was of Horus, and the defeat of Set and his followers by Horus is described with great satisfaction.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.

title.en: The Embrace That Gives Life: The Souls of Osiris and Ra at Busiris
title.zh: 賦生之擁抱：奧西里斯與拉之魂相擁於布西里斯

region.en: Busiris (Tattu), Nile Delta, Egypt (where the souls of Osiris and Ra meet)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲布西里斯（塔圖，二魂相擁之地）

texts.period: Pyramid Texts (Pepi II 568, Teta 268) and Papyrus of Nesi-Amsu; depicted in the Papyrus of Ani (Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, the embrace of Horus and Osiris

summary.en: How life is transferred in Egyptian theology — by embrace: Horus embraces his dead father and so passes to him his own Ka; Isis gathers the flesh, binds the hands and embraces Osiris; Nephthys builds the body in her character of Seshat the architect-goddess; Khepera takes Shu and Tefnut in his arms to give them life; and when Osiris usurped the power of Ra, the souls of the two became one after each had embraced the other at Busiris.
summary.zh: 埃及神學中生命之傳遞——以擁抱：荷魯斯擁亡父，以己卡授之；伊西斯聚肉縛手而擁之；奈芙蒂斯化身為建築女神莎沙特而造其身；凱佩拉亦擁舒與泰芙努特以賜生；及奧西里斯代拉秉權，二魂於布西里斯相擁而為一。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal funerary texts via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Horus first came to Osiris, who was in the state of a dead man, and embraced him. By this embrace he transferred to him either his own Ka (double), or a portion of the power which dwelt in it; the embrace was, in fact, an act whereby something of the vital energy of the embracer was transferred to the embraced. When Isis wished to revivify Osiris she gathered together his flesh, and bound up his hands, and embraced him, and Nephthys took in her arms his flesh when she had gathered it together, and was about to build it into a body in her character of the goddess Seshat, who presided over the planning of buildings.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III.

passages.text: Similarly, when Khepera, the primeval Sun-god, had created Shu and Tefnut, and wished to give them life, he took their forms in his arms, and they became living gods. The life of a god could be absorbed by the king's embracing the statue of the god, and in later times, when Osiris had been made to usurp the power of Ra, the souls of Osiris and Ra became one after each god had embraced the other.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III, citing the Papyrus of Nesi-Amsu and Moret's Ritual.

title.en: The Weighing of Words: Thoth Makes True the Voice of Osiris
title.zh: 言辭之秤：托特使奧西里斯之言成真

region.en: An (Heliopolis), Egypt (the hall of the Aged God, where Set accused Osiris)
region.zh: 埃及赫利奧波利斯（長者神之廳，塞特訟奧西里斯處）

texts.period: Pyramid Texts (Teta 271) and Book of the Dead ch. 18 (Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, the trial of Osiris at An

summary.en: The murder was only Set's first move: he stirred the gods of heaven to bar Osiris from their company and laid formal charges against him; Thoth tried the matter in the hall of the Aged God at An — 'on the night of the battle, on the night of the shackling of the Sebau fiends, and on the day of the destruction of Neb-er-tcher' — a weighing of words in which Thoth 'made true the voice' of Osiris and declared Set the liar; henceforth maa kheru, 'true of voice,' is written after the name of every dead follower of Osiris.
summary.zh: 弒君僅為塞特之始：彼煽惑天神拒奧西里斯於神列之外，並具狀訟之；托特乃於長者神之廳審之——『於戰鬥之夜、於縛塞寶惡靈之夜、於內伯-特切爾滅亡之日』——此乃『言辭之秤』，托特『使其言成真』，而判塞特為謊者；自此凡奧西里斯門下亡者之名後皆書『言真實』（maa kheru）。

sensitivity.note: Ancient theology via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Under the VIth dynasty it was commonly believed that this trial of Osiris took place in the city of An (the On of the Bible), as is clear from the passage in the text of Teta (1. 271), in which the deceased is exhorted to go and 'sit at the head of the gods, and to do what Osiris did in the House of the Prince which is in An.' The same view is taken in the XVIIIth Chapter of the Theban Recension of the Book of the Dead wherein Thoth is thus addressed: 'Hail, Thoth, who didst make Osiris to be victorious over his enemies, make thou... to be victorious over his enemies, as thou didst make Osiris to be victorious over his enemies in the presence of the Tchatcha who are with Ra and Osiris in An, on the night of things of the night, on the night of the battle, on the night of the shackling of the Sebau fiends, and on the day of the destruction of Neb-er-tcher.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III.

passages.text: To these [accusations] Osiris replied, and when Thoth had heard the evidence he summed up the case, and then declared that Osiris had spoken the truth, in fact that it was not he who was a liar, but Set. Thoth held the word of Osiris to be true, or 'made the word true,' as the Egyptian text has it. The trial in the hall at An was, in reality, a 'weighing of words,' the words being the accusations of Set and the defence of Osiris; it was no trial of strength like the fight between Horus and Set, and Ra and Apep. The matter which Thoth had to decide was, Which witness is true, Set or Osiris?
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.

passages.text: When a god, or a man, or a woman, is said to be maa kheru we are to understand that when he or she has spoken, or 'uttered words,' the words are followed immediately by the effect desired, that is to say, he who is maa kheru possessed unlimited power, and there is nothing which he cannot do or obtain. Moreover, Osiris, having been declared true of word, or true of voice, by Thoth, went up into heaven, and reigned there as king. He also became judge of the dead, for all men knew that he had proved Set to be a liar when he was tried by the gods.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.

title.en: The Title-Deed of Horus: The Iron Tablet in the House of Books
title.zh: 荷魯斯之地契：書屋中的鐵版

region.en: The House of Books, Egyptian Other World (symbolic pin, Memphis)
region.zh: 埃及冥界書屋（象徵定位，孟菲斯）

texts.period: Book of the Dead ch. 183, Hymn to Osiris of Hunefer (Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, the succession of Horus

summary.en: The legal machinery of the succession myth: 'The throne of Keb hath been adjudged unto him, along with the rank which hath been established by the god Temu, and also by the title-deed (or, will), in the House of Books, which hath been cut upon an iron tablet according to the command of thy father Ptah-Tanen, when he sat upon the great throne' — Set is set over what Shu bears up, the waters stretched over the high lands, grain made to grow, and 'gods celestial and gods terrestrial transfer themselves to the service of thy son Horus.'
summary.zh: 繼承神話之法律機器：『蓋布之座已判歸於他，連同阿圖姆所立之位，以及書屋中所存之地契（遺囑）——依其父卜塔-坦能於大座之上所命，鐫於鐵版』——塞特受命於舒所舉者之上，水漫高地，五穀生長——『天上地下諸神皆轉而事爾子荷魯斯。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary hymn via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: 'Thy son Horus is triumphant in the presence of the whole company of the gods, the sovereignty of the whole world hath been given unto him, and his dominion is in the uttermost parts of the earth. The throne of Keb (the earth-god) hath been adjudged unto him, along with the rank which hath been established by the god Temu, and also by the title-deed (or, will), in the House of Books, which hath been cut upon an iron tablet according to the command of thy father Ptah-Tanen, [when he sat upon] the great throne.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III, quoting the hymn to Osiris of Hunefer (Book of the Dead ch. 183).

passages.text: 'He hath set his brother over that which the god Shu beareth up [i.e., heaven], and hath made him to stretch out the waters over the high lands, and to cause to grow that which springeth up on the hills, and the grain which groweth up from the earth, and to give increase by water and by land. Gods celestial and gods terrestrial transfer themselves to the service of thy son Horus, and they follow him into the hall, where a decree is passed which declareth that he is their lord, and the gods accept the same straightway.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.

title.en: Isis Great with Child Like the Star Sept
title.zh: 如天狼星而懷孕之伊西斯

region.en: Saut, Egypt (where Isis and Nephthys work the knotted cords)
region.zh: 埃及紹特（伊西斯與奈芙蒂斯行結織法術之地）

texts.period: Pyramid Texts (Teta 275 ff. = Pepi I 28 ff.), 6th Dynasty (Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, the begetting of Horus

summary.en: The oldest text of the miraculous conception: 'Isis and Nephthys work magic on thee with knotted cords in the city of Saut... Thy sister Isis cometh unto thee rejoicing in her love for thee. Thou settest her upon thee, thy issue entereth into her, and she becometh great with child like the star Sept (the Dog-star). Horus-Sept cometh forth from thee in the form of Horus, dweller in Sept. He avengeth thee in his name of Heru-sa-netch-atef' — Horus the avenger of his father.
summary.zh: 神蹟懷孕之最古文本：『伊西斯與奈芙蒂斯於紹特城以結繩行法於爾……爾姊伊西斯欣然懷愛而來。爾置之於上，爾之後嗣入之，彼遂如天狼星塞普特而懷孕。荷魯斯-塞普特自爾而出，形如棲於塞普特之荷魯斯。彼以『復父仇者』之名為爾復仇。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal funerary texts via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: In the text of Teta it is said: 'Isis and Nephthys work magic on thee with knotted cords in the city of Saut, for their lord is in thee in thy name of Neb-Saut (i.e., Lord of Saut), for their god is in thee in thy name of god (Neter). They adore thee; do not depart from them in thy name of Tua-neter (i.e., Morning Star). They present [themselves] before thee; be not wroth in thy name of Tchenteru.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III.

passages.text: 'Thy sister Isis cometh unto thee rejoicing in her love for thee. Thou settest her upon thee, thy issue entereth into her, and she becometh great with child like the star Sept (the Dog-star). Horus-Sept cometh forth from thee in the form of Horus, dweller in Sept. Thou makest him to have a spirit in his name of Spirit, dweller in Tchenteru. He avengeth thee in his name of Heru-sa-netch-atef.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.
